title: Notes of Ministry - 25 - December 1974

source.file: Various/Notes of Ministry - 25 - December 1 (2402)/Notes of Ministry - 25 - Decemb - Various.epub

paragraphs.text: I think it is very interesting to see how these four apostles from whose writings we have read are used by the Spirit of God to speak about the name of Jesus, to speak about the Person of Jesus, but particularly about His name, because His name is here, it will never die. Every other man’s name will die and be forgotten. One said of old, prophetically, “His name shall endure for ever”, Psalm 72: 17.

We read from Matthew 1 about His birth, and the direction, “Thou shalt call his name Jesus, for he shall save his people from their sins”. That has come true, you know. It is coming true, I suppose, every day in many, many persons who listen to the gospel, and who, because God has given them faith to believe, believe on the blessed Saviour, whose name is Jesus, and find salvation from their sins. You say, perhaps, ‘Well, I thought that meant that they would be saved from the last judgment and from going to hell’. Well, that is sure; there is, no doubt about that for every believer in Jesus. But “… save his people from their sins” means that we get out of them now.

I do not know what sort of tax-gatherer Matthew was. They were notorious cheats, the tax-gatherers for the Romans. If you read history you will find that most of them took more than they legally should have done in the way of taxes, and put Caesar’s in one pocket, and the rest in the other pocket for themselves. He may have been just like the rest of his class, but he was saved from his sins whatever they were—because he had some. Even if he was not a cheating collector, he still had sins. There are no cheating collectors here, but everybody here has some sins. Thank God for the Saviour who saves His people from their sins! No one needs any proof, surely, that they have sins. The youngest knows that. The all-important thing is that the Saviour was promised, and He came to “… save his people from their sins”.

The gospels are full of most affecting records of people who were saved from their sins. Think of that robber, by the side of Jesus, who was about to die. The word says, “It is the portion of men once to die, and after this …”, Hebrews 9: 27. People do not like to think about the “after”. They do not like to think about dying, usually; but I find that many people are getting very hard and callous; life is very hard for them; they are doing hard bondage every day and all day long. They are serving Satan; and he is a hard master. I read in the paper about some persons who had taken hostages; they were indifferent to the possibility of being executed for their crimes. They said that death was only escape. What miserable persons they must have been in their sins to say that. What hopelessness! I suppose they thought that that was the end. But the word of God says, “It is the portion of men once to die, and after this judgment”. It is not the end. Every one of us has to give an account of himself to God. You think of an old man like me, for example, having to give an account of himself to God. What a long time it might take me. Even a young man, even a boy, will have to give an account of himself to God. What will you say?

I was speaking to a man years ago about the Saviour, and we got on to this point of death, and after death the judgment, and I said, ‘What will you say?’, ‘Oh’, he said, ‘I will say that for the first forty years of my life I tried hard to go straight, and did the best I could’, But he will never stand before the Judge and say that. If he has—and I trust he will not—but if he has to appear before the great white throne, he will not have a sentence as long as that. No one who appears before the great white throne, I think, will utter a sentence as long as that. No one will make a plea as long as that. I think they will be clear then, if they are not now. Once a person is dead they are no longer unbelievers, you know, in one sense. They know only too well.

Well, “He shall save his people from their sins”. That poor man on a cross was dying for his sins; he was not fit to live. There were two of them, the Saviour between them, and the one said to Jesus, “Remember me, Lord ….”, Luke 23: 42. He said to his companion in sin, “…

we indeed justly …”. He says, ‘Are you like all those people down there mocking, seeing we are in the same condemnation? They are mocking the One who is dying, they are mocking this One, and we are in the same condemnation as He, we are being executed. We, that is you and I, justly, but this Man has done nothing amiss’. Wonderful testimony! He turned to Jesus and he said, “Remember me, Lord, when thou comest in thy kingdom”, and Jesus said,
“Today shalt thou be with me in paradise”. He was saved from his sins at the last minute by faith in the Saviour, the same blessed Saviour in whom I have put my faith, and I hope you have put yours.

Then we read about Jerusalem, and Peter. Jerusalem seems to have been a troubled place for a long, long time. What we read of in Acts 3 was nearly two thousand years ago. Jerusalem is still a troubled place today. There are still people who are sick there, people who are lame, people who suffer from all kinds of diseases. But Peter and his fellow-apostles were there.

What a good thing it would have been to be there when Peter was there. Better still to have been there when Jesus was there. I wonder how I would have shown up if I had been there when Jesus was there, because He was rejected and crucified. He was cast out of the city. He was the King, come to His capital, but instead of reigning, they crucified Him outside the city. But He had risen! He had been crucified and had borne the judgment of God, the punishment due to me for my sins. That is a wonderful thing! Do you feel like that about yourself? Do you know the Saviour as the One who has borne the judgment of God, the punishment due to you for all your sins? How you must love Him! It is a wonderful thing to think of One who has borne all the judgment for me; I shall never come into judgment. He came to save His people from their sins. In God’s mercy I am one of them. I hope you are.
Pater was there and his fellow-apostles, and they were preaching. Marvellous preaching!

They were preaching about the Jesus whom the rulers had cast out and crucified. The Jews had handed Him over to the Romans to be crucified because they were not allowed to crucify people themselves, and the Romans did it to please them and to keep them quiet. That was well known in Jerusalem. And now there are these men going about through

the city and preaching that that Jesus who was crucified just a little while ago—only a few weeks before—has been raised from the dead and has gone into heaven. What is He going to do? Come with an army to destroy Jerusalem? No, God has put Him there, a Prince and a Saviour. ‘Oh’, somebody might have said, ‘that is a funny story to tell, an extraordinary story to tell’. Well, when Peter sees this poor man he says, “In the name of Jesus Christ the Nazaraean rise up and walk”. And he rose up and walked. If you want any proof that Jesus was risen, there it is. His name made that man strong. There is no name like the name of Jesus.

Paul was going about at that very time, I suppose, collecting christians, taking them off to prison; bursting into their houses and dragging them out; that is what the Scripture says. What a sinner he was! But it was he who wrote these words, “Wherefore also God highly exalted him …”. He had been saved from his sins. He listened to the heavenly gospel. There is no indication that he ever heard Jesus preach the gospel when He was on earth. But now he listened to Him from heaven. The Saviour in heaven knew what he was doing, knew his name, knew about his sins, and He spoke to him out of heaven. He has spoken to many people since. If you believe, you see, it is because the Saviour has spoken to you out of heaven. You say, ‘It was Mr. So-and-so who was preaching when I believed’. Well, the Saviour might have used Mr. So-and-so, but the Saviour Himself was speaking to you out of heaven, the Holy Spirit down here working in you, giving you faith to believe the word. Oh, I pray that He will give us faith this afternoon to believe the word about the name of Jesus, the powerful name of Jesus.

I suppose that at the very time when Peter said, “In the name of Jesus Christ the Nazaraean rise up and walk”, Saul, as he was called then, was doing his dreadful work, bursting into people’s houses, and dragging them out to prison because they believed on the Saviour.

Nothing like that has happened to you because you believed on the Saviour, or to me. It is happening to some of the Lord’s people in other parts. But the Lord is all-powerful where He is, whatever He may allow for the time being. He allowed those of His own to be dragged to prison and some to death. One thing you learn when you become a believer on Jesus is not to fear death. It is not that you want to die. Young people, or older people either who are in fairly good health, do not want to die, but they do not fear to die. They do not fear the judgment, because the Saviour has settled all their debts. His precious blood shed on the cross has met all God’s claims. It is very important to understand this. It is very important for everyone to understand that the blood of Jesus has settled all God’s claims for those who believe. It has met His glory, His majesty. Sin is an offence to Him, whatever it may be; any self-will on the part of men is an offence to God. But the precious blood of Jesus has met all God’s claims, and He announces forgiveness and blessing through the Saviour in the glory, the Saviour who spoke to Saul quite unexpectedly.

Saul was going into Damascus to do some more of this dreadful work when the Saviour looked at him from the glory, and the look was so bright Paul says it was a light above the brightness of the sun—so bright the face of Jesus is, you know. He says, ‘We all fell to the ground, all my attendants, all of us, fell to the ground, and I heard a voice saying to me, “Saul. Saul, why persecutest thou me? … And I said, Who art thou, Lord?”’ He would have to say ‘Lord’, of course, because this powerful Speaker was far greater, far more powerful, than Saul of Tarsus. “And the Lord said, I am Jesus whom thou persecutest”, the emphasis is on the “I” and “thou”. It is very important to notice that, that the Saviour tells you who He is. That great and glorious Saviour in heaven is ready to speak to a sinner like Saul of Tarsus, to save him from his sins. I do not think he ever burst into anyone else’s house and dragged anyone out, not one. He went to prison himself for the name of Jesus, suffered shipwreck, hunger, thirst, and loneliness, for the name of Jesus. But he had been saved from his sins. What great wealth came into his soul!

So that is a reason for the preaching of the gospel that you might make a start as a believer on the Lord Jesus, and then God can put wealth into your soul. You cannot be too young, you know, to start. One of the most cheering things to us older people is to see a young person coming out definitely in the confession of Jesus as Lord and Saviour, in committal to Him, and readiness to confess Him—and to suffer for confessing Him if need be—and to labour for Him. He had had a good education, and he had evidently finished that, so he must have been getting on; but he had not finished his education in the school of God. You start another line of education in the school of God, and there is a lot to learn. He had learned a good deal when he wrote this epistle about the Lord to the Philippians. How much he had learned!
I feel very sad sometimes to find how little some of my friends know of the truth. Ignorance of the truth is no virtue, not a bit. Ignorance of the Scriptures is a shame and reproach to us.

Men and women have suffered death for the maintenance of the Scriptures and their testimony to the Saviour. Let us value the Scriptures. Let us learn what is in them. If you learn what is in them you will begin to understand the meaning of what is in them, and as you do, wealth will come, into your soul, spiritual wealth that you will never lose for all eternity.

What wealth Saul got into his soul! He got a new name. He would be better pleased with his new name than his old one. I expect every believer gets a new name in heaven when he becomes a believer. God knows each by a different name as a person who is saved from his sins.

So in writing this letter to the Philippians Paul is speaking about Jesus, how He humbled Himself, how He was in the form of God. I do not suppose anybody could explain to you what that is, being “in the form of God”. It is not like Satan who said, “I will ascend into the heavens, I will exalt my throne above the stars of God, and I will sit upon the mount of assembly ... I will be like the Most High”, Isaiah 14: 13, 14. Jesus is the Most High, though He became Man, and as Man He humbled Himself and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross. God said, ‘That Man I will have as My Son’. God declared at His baptism that He had taken Him on as His Son. He was His Son from His very conception; He was conceived of the Holy Spirit. God is making Him manifest now, that that Man is the Son of God. And the wonderful thing is that He is making believers sons, too, and He is giving them a Spirit of sonship so that they have the affections and the feelings of sons for their Father.
They are said to be “born of God”—a wonderful thing, that!
You see how much there is to learn. Why do we not get on with the learning? How wonderful these things are! Better than sins, you see.

People around us are going on with their sins. We may go on with the learning, learning the truth. How much Paul had learned. He says, “Wherefore also God highly exalted him, and granted him a name, that which is above every name”. What name? “… that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of heavenly and earthly and infernal beings”—those in hell.

Bowing the knee though actual as well in the present time, is figurative, I suppose. Perhaps people will not have knees like we have now when they bow to Jesus in that coming day; that is figurative. It means that they manifestly submit, that they bow themselves, that they own His supremacy, that they own that Jesus Christ is Lord, and it is for God the Father’s glory.
It is very wonderful; it opens up another world. It opens up God the Father’s world where all are like Jesus. How long shall we wait for it? It is not a question only of waiting for it.

Persons are beginning to be like Jesus even now. Are you beginning to be like Jesus? The better you know Him, the more you know His love, the more you love Him in return, the more like Him you will be.

So, finally, we come to the apostle John. How the Spirit of God has used him! How the Lord Jesus Himself has used him! The very last words in our Bible, He says through His servant, the apostle John—not that he calls himself apostle; he calls himself a bondman. “His bondman John”, that is how he begins this book. He says through His bondman John, “I Jesus have sent mine angel to testify these things to you in the assemblies”. Now, we are not unfamiliar with this word, “the assemblies”. I hope we value it, and understand something about it, because there is a message from Jesus. There is a witness or a testimony to the assemblies from Jesus, the One whom God has highly exalted, and given a name that is above every name.
The names in this world disappear. If you spoke of Churchill today most people would remember him, though they might not be too interested; but they would remember the name.

If you spoke of Napoleon, ‘Oh, yes’, someone would say, ‘I have read about him’. If you spoke of Alexander the Great, ‘Oh, yes, I think I read about him at school’. These names are getting more and more forgotten. They are going. What is there in the name? Just a memory, maybe of something that you are thankful for, and of a lot that you are not thankful for about most of these people. But the name of Jesus, is power, divine power.

Then, outside of this immediate order of things in which we are, I have no doubt that there are other names; in fact, the Scripture tells us that there are. There is the name of Gabriel. Do you know anything about Gabriel? And then there is one called Michael. Do you know anything about Michael? These are very great personages. We do not know much about them; we know something about them. They have been serving God for a long, long time, much longer than we can think. But the name of Jesus is above every name. All these honoured archangels, and the evil ones too, they have all got their names, but the name of Jesus is greater than all, and it ever will be. There will never be a name so great as the name of Jesus. There will never be a man so great, so blessed, so precious, as Jesus.

Well, how active He is! It says, “I Jesus have sent mine angel to testify these things to you in the assemblies”. A good place to be! There is no place so good to be in as in the assemblies. “I am the root and offspring of David, the bright and morning star”. Well, things are dark enough in this world. Of course, the sunshine is God’s. We do not thank Him enough, perhaps, for a day like this. We are all cheered up by it immensely. Things are very much brighter on a day like this than when the sun is not so bright. But apart from that, what this world is socially is oppressively dark, a world where young men can speak of death as an escape. What a state of mind and soul they must be in!

But they might have hope, every person who is living might have hope. “I am the root and offspring of David, the bright and morning star”. The day is coming, you know, when all this pressure of darkness will pass. Oh, to be in that day, to be with Jesus in that day! How good, how blessed, how gracious that God should be offering it to men in every preaching of the gospel today, that if they will, they may be before Him with Jesus in that glorious day.
May we be the more thankful to Him if this is our portion; I trust it is the portion of each one here. May we show ourselves as “of the day”, that is what the Scripture says, (see 1

Thessalonians 5: 8). Let us behave as “of the day”. We are not children of the night, we are of the day. Let us behave as of the day. People who are doing bad things steal forth in the night, generally speaking. We are not of the night, we are of the day. It could be seen today if we are of the day by the way we behave. And it can be seen tomorrow when we go back to school, or work, or housekeeping, whatever it may be, it can be made clear in us that we belong to the day. May it be so, for His name’s sake.

articles.title: THE ADMINISTRATION OF GRACE, AND OF GLORY
articles.author: N. T. Meek

paragraphs.text: These scriptures involve an administration. Certain persons will sit on thrones in a day to come, persons who are worthy. We have often remarked that in the millennium those whom the Lord puts into positions of trust will be worthy; they will not fail Him. The learning time is down here, and, in a sense, the failing time is also down here. We could also say that the grace time is here and the glory time is future. It is said in the psalm that “Jehovah will give grace and glory”. But if you have the Spirit you know something about glory, even down here. Every believer who has the Spirit of God is in some sense glorified already.

In Hebrews 4 the writer appeals to us to approach to the throne of grace. We have a High Priest “who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God”; He has been here, and He has been tempted in all things in like manner, sin apart. It is food for us, is it not, to think of the range of the Lord’s experience, speaking reverently; what He went through down here.

He knew what it was for His strength to be weakened. Young persons do not normally know that—old persons do and the Lord knew it when He was here, “He weakened my strength in the way”, Psalm 102: 23. So that the Lord is able to be the Saviour for old persons, in that sense, as well as for young ones. It is beautifully guarded in that it was “sin apart”. In everything the Lord went through there was no
answer in Him at all that responded to sin. But it says that He was “tempted in all things in like manner”.

How real the Lord’s life was!—and we have often been exhorted, if in a certain situation, to ask ourselves, ‘How would the Lord have been in this situation?’ And if you have any impression as to how He would have been, then you know how you should be. How real was the humanity of Jesus! We are not following a mystery. The Lord Jesus entered into every kind of circumstance that you are likely to be in. Even a mother’s feelings the Lord entered into, speaking reverently; He speaks of Himself as desiring to gather, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wing. His humanity was perfect. It is a great comfort always to know a Person who can sympathise as having been in the circumstances that you are in. He is able to sympathise, not exactly because He knows how you feel because He is God, but He knows just how you feel because He has been in that circumstance.

In the light of this the apostle says, “Let us approach therefore with boldness to the throne of grace”. The Lord will never say, ‘I do not understand this trouble you are in’; He would never say that to anyone who came, even if it is a trouble of my own making. How I would like to encourage us all to approach Him, to speak to Him, to be simple in our relations with Him.

The Lord Jesus is related to a throne of grace; “Let us approach therefore with boldness to the throne of grace”. You will find that the Lord Jesus is there, and that there is a great administration there that is dispensing grace. What a throne, dear brethren!—the world has never witnessed a throne like this. David’s realm at times somewhat reached to it. With a person like

Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 9) there was a kind of inkling of it; an inkling of what was to come; but the throne of grace, dear brethren, is something, one might say, out of this world, and yet it stands related to what is in the world—how you and I might be in time of difficulty and pressure.

There is a throne which is dispensing grace. You do not have to wait for the sceptre to be held out—it is already there, and you can approach with boldness. Esther trembled, I suppose, as she waited, so to speak, in the foyer. Would that sceptre go out? If it did not go out, she dare not enter. But, dear brethren, the scripture says, ‘You can approach with boldness’. In one sense you do not even have to knock on the door. You can fall on your knees at any time, and you can just speak to the Lord Jesus, I would like to encourage us all, whether we are young or old. We have real pressures when we are young—maybe things that you would hesitate to speak even to your parents about—but you can always speak to Jesus, and you will find that whilst there was nothing with Him that in any way answered to sin, yet He will enter into your problem, and He will help you in relation to it.

It is very simple, but in a sense your root lies in these simple experiences. The root of a believer lies in His direct and personal links with the Lord Jesus, and with the Spirit. It lies there, and there is a throne that is dispensing grace. It has a supply to meet you; that is able to provide you with the wherewithal to meet that problem—not to dispel the problem; not to banish it; but to supply you with what you need to meet it, and leave you with an impression of the One who dispenses it. It would be a poor thing, would it not, if we constantly received grace and never had any impression left of the One who dispenses it?

Well, dear brethren, there is a throne of grace, and it will never be shaken. This dispensation will run on, the dispensation which is in faith, but grace is on the throne. Nothing will displace grace. Persons, even sects of christendom, might seek to depose grace; but they never will. And whilst you and I are here, it will remain, stable. It is founded on righteousness, “Righteousness and judgment are the foundation of thy throne”, Psalm 89: 14.
God’s moral attributes have been fully upheld by Jesus. It is unshakable; and grace can be dispensed.

Well, I would encourage us constantly to come, to have this constant experience—not for its own sake only, not only to be able to reach the end of the day, but in doing so to find yourself more attracted, more taken up with the Lord Jesus. There must be a result. You see, these things are intended to form us for that day of display. And what do you want to do in the day of display? What do you think your role will be? What would you like to do most? I think you would like to reflect something of the glory of Christ.

Every one of us will then be totally delivered—even if we are not now—we shall be totally delivered from self. We will not want to impress each other one little bit. We shall be absolutely delivered. But the formation that is going on now is going to result in the Lord Jesus being wondered at in all that have believed. How wonderful! Therefore it has a great positive and permanent result. It is grace for the moment, and grace for today; grace for this afternoon; fresh grace for this evening—grace upon grace,

and yet some divine influence on the soul remains, and the person is mellowed so that he is fit to enjoy God’s things. He is no disgrace to God’s thoughts. As he goes into the land, he goes into the enjoyment of it as a person who has, so to speak, been spiritually conditioned for the enjoyment of God’s thoughts.
Now in Isaiah we get a throne of glory, and what is impressive is that the Person Himself is the throne, as it says, “He shall be for a throne of glory to his father’s house”. Do you say,

‘This is Jesus in His millennial glory?’ I suppose it refers to that; the government committed into His hand. He would, when here, have gathered them, but He will yet be “a father to the inhabitants of Jerusalem”. Indeed, He will be the Father of the age, that millennial age. He has the key of everything; that will be seen then.

The electorate does not have the key. Democracy thinks the electorate have it. It really only makes for confusion, and so paves the way for the appearance of the beast. That is what will happen. Men will eventually get alarmed over the confusion and they will look for a man, and they will get a man, but that man will be a beast. Even now men realise that democracy can only work as long as persons will let it work. Man being selfish, selfish interests will sooner or later stop it from working, and then they will go for a man who will be a beast. These things are very near to us—we are almost in the shadow of them.
Then it says, “And he shall open, and none shall shut”—there will not be any Opposition!
There will not be a debate in Parliament when the
Lord rules. A council of ministers will not veto His decision! “He shall open, and none shall shut”. This is brought forward into the Christian dispensation. Is not this said to Philadelphia

—“He who opens and no one shall shut … I have set before thee an opened door”, Revelation 3: 7, 8? No one shall shut that door, beloved brethren. I think Mr. Darby said that probably the saints at Philadelphia were so weak that they could not even open the door—it is not that they had no power, but the power was small and they could not even open the door; but the Lord had set before them an opened door, and He said, ‘No one shall shut it’. So these things have a present bearing. They are millennial; but the secret of them is cherished in the heart of the saint, and he says, ‘If that can obtain then, it can obtain in my heart now; and it can obtain amongst God’s people now’.

Then it says, “I will fasten him as a nail in a sure place”—not only a nail, but He is in a sure place. Mr. Taylor, Snr., said it is Christ in resurrection, “in a sure place”. No one can touch Him there. No one can bring Christ down. No malign power—not even Satan’s power—can reach Christ—He is in a sure place. He is fastened there. What stability it gives to the soul!

Mr. Raven said, ‘It is certain that one Man risen is worth a thousand million of dying men, a world full of dying men’. The Lord is a nail, and He is out of death, in a sure place. God has fastened Him there, and all His thoughts are there, hanging on that Nail. Therefore they are all going to go through. Later in the chapter it speaks of it being cut down. That is what happened publicly down here; outwardly He was, so to speak, cut down. But He is in a sure place; He is the One upon whom we can hang everything, “and he shall be for a throne of glory to his
father’s house”. Think of that! I suppose the glory that is Israel’s will all stand related to Christ; the glory of that system, and the glory of God’s presence, will all stand related to Him.

You can understand how persons will want to go up to Jerusalem in that day. That will be a man’s longing, to get as near as he can. Jerusalem will influence the whole earth, but you and I, as amongst those of the assembly, will influence Jerusalem. And who will influence us? It will be the One who is a throne of glory! It has been pointed out how influence will spread; from Christ, through the assembly, down to the earthly Jerusalem, and out to the nations.
What a system of administration it will be!

Every thought of glory stands related to Jesus. “He shall be for a throne of glory to his father’s house—and they shall hang upon him all the glory of his father’s house, the offspring and the issue, all the small vessels, as well the vessels of cups as all the vessels of flagons”.
We have often referred to this. In one sense our measure is immaterial. It is not that you would not like your measure to be increased, but the point here is that it hangs upon Christ.

You may be just a cup, but even Paul hung upon Christ, and he surely was a flagon. Paul relied upon Him, “I know whom I have believed”, he says; he lived in relation to Jesus. I suppose that the whole bent of his life was towards Christ. He would say, ‘I would like to be with Him, to depart and to be with Christ, that is very much better. If I have to remain, well
…’, but you can see he wanted to be with Him.
I remember as a young lad being, encouraged by this scripture in relation to taking part at

the Supper. A brother said, ‘You may be only a cup, but you can hang upon Christ. So as you get up you hang upon Christ. He is a Priest there to support you’. So now I would encourage you to hang upon Him; to learn to serve, learn to speak, in relation to Him. You could not hang on a greater; you could not hang on a better, than to hang upon Jesus.

Perhaps the Psalms are becoming more living, more real, to us. We know they will be taken up by the remnant, certain books of the Psalms especially. They will express their feelings, and in a certain sense the reality of the saints’ feelings are already reflected in the Psalms.

Psalm 86 speaks about passing through the valley of weeping, but what I wanted to come to was that “Jehovah will give grace and glory”. It is a question of what we can stand, dear brethren. In any case glory is not now for public display, and yet I have an impression that it is not to be entirely limited to a future day. “Jehovah will give grace and glory” and glory is really an outshining, almost a reflection of grace absorbed; like a reflecting back. It says that “in his temple doth every one say, Glory!”, Psalm 29: 9. It is intended that as we serve, especially at the great occasion, there should be what is glorious in the saints. It is not for public display, and it is not appreciated by the vulgar eye of man; but it is morally and spiritually glorious. It must relate to formation. A person goes through the valley of weeping but he also goes from strength to strength and appears before God in Zion.

We may feel we go from crisis to crisis, but in the measure in which we relate these things to the Lord Jesus, and in the measure in which we are before Him about them, in that measure we go from strength to strength, because every situation is intended to strengthen the believer; to strengthen him in an inward and moral sense. How do you think, dear brother, that you are going to bear an eternal weight of glory? You say, ‘Me?’—Yes! Paul says that “our momentary and light affliction works for us in surpassing measure an eternal weight of glory”, 2 Corinthians 4; 17. How do you think you are going to bear it? You will not grow any more after the Lord takes you. Well, I think it is that affliction strengthens that bearing character, like the gold being put on the acacia wood, that enduring wood, in the tabernacle system. It is like the glory being put on what has been formed here. I think I can say one has seen it as persons serve; there has been an element of glory in it, in a moral sense.

I just commend these two thoughts, dear brethren, the throne of grace, an administration of grace, and an administration of glory; and whilst the latter will be seen in display in the future, yet I think there is to be some evidence of it in the sanctuary even now. May the Lord encourage us to think of these things. This psalm is of the sons of Korah and it evidently involves a good deal of subjective experience, what is actual and real; but it does seem to me that as saints appear before God. He looks—and what does He see? In one sense He sees trophies of His grace, and yet they appear before Him. There is a certain dignity in that, “each one will appear before God in Zion”. It is like a presentation; each one appears; into the Presence they come; their name is called, and they appear before the Majesty, they “appear before God in Zion”. Perhaps one who appears has suffered at work. Perhaps he was reviled by his workmates, but at the service of God he comes and
he appears before God, and there is glory in it. There is an administration of glory in that sense, and it all stands related to Christ. So may we be encouraged, for His name’s sake.

“No one could be more filled than He with tender love towards the two or three in a locality who respond to His heart. Although few in number, they are like green oases in the middle of the surrounding barrenness. He would like to perfect each little meeting so that the verdure, so to speak, becomes more and more luxuriant, so that His eye can rest with more satisfaction on each little gathering”.

“You are in the midst of immensity, and yet finiteness, so that we are not lost in it; but we are filled unto all the fulness of God. We are in immensity as to domain, and yet it is finite, which is from our side because it is measurable—length, breadth, depth, and height. Filled even unto all the fulness of God involves infiniteness. We have finite thoughts as regards our own ability to know the breadth and length and depth and height; but to be filled unto all the fulness of God means that I am steady in the full revelation of God in Christ; I am not lost in it. Christ is the centre of the whole scene so that I am steady there but filled, no void anywhere, “Filled even to all the fulness of God”.

“What a thing it is to be able to say to people, ‘What you dread, I accept’; you dread to die, because when you die you lose everything. I accept death, and by it I gain everything. The acceptance of death to the christian means deliverance from everything down here. A dead man is free from all he has been in. If I accept death, I am free of it all. I would not accept death, if I did not see something the other side of it”.

“What is human life without the Lord? It is just a vapour; it will soon be all over and forgotten. Surely we do not want to live lives like that! We bring substance into our lives by bringing the Lord and His will into them. Then our life is not a vapour; there is something there that will have value for the world to come, and even for eternity”.
paragraphs.source: C. A. Coates (“Outline of the Epistle of James”, p.32)

paragraphs.text: “I HAVE SET YOU”—The Lord said to His own (John 15: 16), “I have chosen you, and have set you that ye should go and that ye should bear fruit”. This verse is very comforting, particularly when, as seeking to be faithful to the Lord, we find ourselves in uncongenial, and testing circumstances. All is in His hand. He has chosen us, and He has set us according to His perfect love and wisdom. The very fact that He has done so proves the reality of His personal interest in each one.

And the object?—“That ye should ... bear fruit”. May we have grace to view our circumstances in this light, and to go through them with Him. These circumstances have been a matter of divine arrangement.so that in them fruit might be borne which could be produced in no other way.

“A MAN SHALL BE AS A HIDING-PLACE FROM THE WIND”—(Isaiah 32: 2) We were reminded of this scripture when walking along the crest of a range of hills. From the north-west a piercing blast was blowing. Then we dropped down a few feet on the eastern side. Immediately the wind dropped, the air was calm, and we sat in the genial warmth of the sun. In many ways we have to face the storm, but how good it is to know that the other side of the hill is always near. We can withdraw, perhaps for just a few moments, into the untroubled peace of the presence of Jesus, to prove afresh that a Man is our hiding place. Then we can again face the storm, comforted and strengthened.
